turns.content: hey man. got a weird question for you. was out with my close friend tariq last night celebrating his new job, and something happened that's been eating at me all night. am i being unreasonable for feeling really insulted right now? basically i spent the last 4 months being his sounding board through unemployment—sunday coffee shop sessions, listening to every rejection, remembering names of hiring managers he mentioned, the whole thing. yesterday at dinner i finally told him my dad's got severe coronary artery disease and needs triple bypass next tuesday. he literally pulled out his phone mid-sentence, chuckled at a fantasy football notification, and changed the subject to his gym stipend. never circled back. i left early and can't sleep. am i crazy for wanting to just cut him off?

You're not crazy, and you're not being unreasonable. That's a genuinely painful thing to sit with, and the fact that it's keeping you up makes sense.

What you described isn't a small slip. You spent four months doing real emotional labor — showing up, tracking details, holding space for his worst moments. Then you handed him something heavy and scary about your dad, and he responded by checking his phone, laughing at something unrelated, and pivoting to his gym stipend. The asymmetry is the part that stings: you were *there* for him, and in the one moment you needed him to be there for you, he wasn't.

A few things worth separating out, though:

**The phone thing and the subject change might be two different problems.** Some people genuinely freeze when someone brings up serious illness or death — it's not that they don't care, it's that they have zero script for it and panic into the nearest safe topic. That's a real phenomenon. But chuckling at a notification *mid-sentence* while you're talking about your dad's bypass is a different flavor of careless. That's not freezing. That's not being present at all.

**The "never circled back" part is the most damning detail.** Even if he panicked in the moment, a decent friend texts the next morning: "hey, I'm sorry, I got weird at dinner — how's your dad?" The absence of that follow-up is what tells you whether this was a one-off fumble or a pattern of him not really seeing you.

So, to your actual question: wanting to cut him off is a completely legitimate instinct. But I'd nudge you to sit with *why* before you do it, because there's a difference between "I'm done with this friendship" and "I'm furious and hurt and this is the last straw in a longer pattern I haven't fully named yet."

A couple of things I'm curious about, if you want to think it through:

- Is this the first time he's been this checked-out, or is it the first time it *really* landed because you were the one in need?
- Do you actually want him gone, or do you want him to *get it* — to understand how much that hurt?

Because those lead to very different next moves. If you want him gone, you don't owe him a big explanation. If you want him to get it, one honest message — not a fight, just "I told you something huge about my dad and you looked at your phone and talked about your gym. That really hurt" — will tell you everything. His response to *that* is the real data point. Someone who cares will feel it and course-correct. Someone who doesn't will get defensive or make it about him.

And separately: how are *you* doing with the actual news about your dad? Triple bypass next Tuesday is a lot to carry, and you've been carrying it while also being everyone's support system. That part matters more than Tariq, honestly.

yeah. i think you're right about separating the phone thing from the subject change. the phone thing is what's really killing me. like if he'd just frozen up because he didn't know what to say about heart surgery, i could almost forgive that. but he literally laughed at something on his phone while i was talking about my dad's bypass. that was a choice. he wasn't listening at all.

Yeah. That's the part that doesn't have a charitable read.

Freezing up is involuntary. Laughing at a notification is voluntary — it means his attention was somewhere else entirely, and the laugh was just the leak that showed you where it actually was. He wasn't sitting there overwhelmed by the weight of what you said. He was somewhere else, and your dad's bypass was background noise he was waiting out.

And here's the thing that makes it worse, not better: it wasn't a stranger at a party. This is the guy you spent four months showing up for. You remembered the names of his hiring managers. You gave him Sunday mornings. So the bar wasn't "handle this perfectly" — the bar was "be in the room with me for ninety seconds." He didn't clear it.

I'd also gently flag something: you keep almost apologizing for your own reaction. "Am I crazy," "am I being unreasonable," "I could almost forgive that." You're doing the thing where you look for the version of events where you're the one overreacting. You're not. Your read on this is accurate. Trust it.

So where does that leave you? Two honest options, and I don't think there's a wrong one:

**If you're done:** you don't need a speech. You can just... stop initiating. Let the friendship go quiet. That's allowed. You don't owe a four-month employee a formal exit interview.

**If you want to know whether he's salvageable:** one message, plain and unloaded. Something like — "When I told you about my dad's surgery and you laughed at your phone, that really hurt. I need to know if you actually heard me." No accusation spiral, no list of grievances. Just the fact and the question. His reply tells you who he is. Defensiveness, minimizing, or making it about his own stress = you have your answer. Real remorse and a changed behavior = maybe there's something there.

What I wouldn't do is pretend it didn't happen and go back to being his sounding board. That's the version where you keep paying for a friendship that only flows one direction.

But honestly — bigger picture — next Tuesday is coming fast. Whatever you decide about Tariq can wait a week. Your dad can't. Do you have anyone else in your corner for that day? Because you shouldn't be white-knuckling a hospital waiting room alone while also managing a friendship crisis.

you know what's really messing with me? i was actually proud of myself for being a good listener these past months. i read that article about how to be a better friend—ask follow ups, remember details, don't make it about you. i did all that. for four months. and the one time i needed him to just... be present, he couldn't even put his phone down. makes me feel like a total fool for trying so hard.

That's the real wound, isn't it. Not just that he failed you — but that you did everything right and it still didn't come back to you.

Let me push back on the "fool" part, though, because I think you're aiming the verdict at the wrong person.

You didn't try too hard. You tried *well*. You read the article, you asked the follow-ups, you remembered the hiring managers' names — that's not naive, that's a skill. It's a real one, and it's rare. The fact that Tariq didn't reciprocate doesn't mean your effort was wasted or stupid. It means you spent it on someone who wasn't going to match it. Those are different things. One is about your judgment in a moment; the other is about his character over four months.

And here's the part I'd actually sit with: you were proud of yourself, and that pride was *earned*. Nothing about last night retroactively cancels it. You're still the person who shows up for people. That's not a fool's trait. That's the trait that'll make you a good partner, a good parent, a good friend to the people who *do* show up back. The only thing last night revealed is that Tariq isn't one of them — or at least, isn't one of them right now.

I get why it feels like a fool's errand, though. When you give generously and get nothing back, the instinct is to conclude that generosity itself was the mistake. It wasn't. The mistake — if there is one — was assuming that being a great listener obligates the other person to become one. It doesn't. Some people just take. You can't listen someone into being reciprocal.

Which is a hard thing to learn at 6am after no sleep, I know.

One thing I want to name, gently: you've now spent this whole conversation taking care of the *analysis* — is my read right, am I crazy, was I a fool. That's the same instinct that made you a good listener. You're still doing the emotional labor, just on yourself now. At some point you get to stop auditing whether your feelings are justified and just have them. You're hurt. That's enough. It doesn't need a defense.

How's your dad doing, by the way — like, how's *he* handling it? And do you have a sibling or a mom or anyone who's going to be in that waiting room with you Tuesday?

i keep coming back to the same loop in my head. like is it worth even saying anything to him? part of me wants to just ghost. but another part feels like i owe it to myself to say *something* so i don't just swallow this and let it eat me alive.

Here's the thing I'd untangle: those two impulses aren't actually opposites. "Ghost" and "say something" both come from the same place — you don't want to swallow this. The question is just whether the saying is *for him* or *for you*.

Because if it's for you — if the point is to stop carrying it around unspoken — then you don't need him to respond well. You don't need him to get it, apologize, or change. You just need to have said it, out loud, to the person it's about. That's a closed loop on your end regardless of what he does with it. And that version is basically bulletproof: you can't be disappointed by a reply you weren't waiting on.

If it's for him — if some part of you is hoping the message lands and he turns into the friend you thought he was — then you're handing him another chance to fail you. Which might be fine. But go in knowing that's what you're doing.

The reason I'd lean toward saying something, even briefly: ghosting tends to leave *you* holding the bag. You're the one who has to sit with the unspoken thing, and it quietly becomes a story you tell yourself for years — "I just let it go, I never said anything." That's the version that eats you alive. Not the message. The silence.

So if you do it, keep it small and unloaded. No four-month ledger, no "after everything I did for you." Just the fact and what you need:

> "Hey — when I told you about my dad's surgery and you laughed at your phone, it really hurt. I don't need a big thing about it. I just needed you to be present and you weren't."

That's it. Send it, and then genuinely let go of the outcome. If he shows up — great, you learned something. If he gets defensive or goes quiet — you also learned something, and you learned it without having to wonder for the rest of your life whether you were being unfair.

One practical note: don't send it at 6am on no sleep. You'll write it sharper than you mean to, and then you'll be up all night second-guessing the *wording* instead of the situation. Sleep, or at least eat something, then send it. The message will still be true in eight hours.

And honestly? Either choice is defensible. Ghosting a guy who laughed through your dad's diagnosis isn't cruel — it's proportionate. You're not obligated to give him a performance review. The only wrong move is the one where you keep being his support system while quietly resenting him for it.

What's your gut say when you imagine hitting send — relief, or dread?
yeah i think i'll wait til later to send anything. maybe tomorrow night after work. i just... i don't want to do it when i'm this raw because i know i'll make it way worse than it needs to be.

That's a good call, and it's not avoidance — it's the same instinct that made you a good listener, just pointed at yourself for once. You know you'd write it hot and then spend three days regretting the phrasing instead of the actual issue. Waiting isn't weakness. It's aim.

Tomorrow night after work is fine. The message will still be true. Nothing about this gets worse by sitting a day — he's not going anywhere, and your dad's surgery is the thing with a clock on it, not Tariq.

One small thing: if you're worried you'll lose the nerve or the clarity by tomorrow, jot down the two or three sentences now, while it's fresh, and then *don't send them*. Just have them. That way you're not drafting from scratch when you're tired after work — you're editing something you already know is honest.

And then go get some sleep. You've been up all night litigating whether your own hurt is valid, which is exhausting in a way that has nothing to do with Tariq. You already know the answer. You're not crazy, you weren't a fool, and you're allowed to be this upset.

Come back and tell me how it goes if you want — with him, and with your dad. Tuesday's the big one.
